implementation_notes: Rust fuses the two steps into the container: Vec::retain 'Retains only the elements specified by the predicate ... This method operates in place, visiting each element exactly once in the original order, and preserves the order of the retained elements' - it drops the rejected elements while moving the survivors down and fixes the length itself, so the STL's algorithm-plus-erase pair has no counterpart (an algorithm over &mut [T] cannot shorten the vector, which is the borrow-checked echo of the C++ motivation). retain_mut (Rust 1.61) passes the survivor a &mut T so it can be updated while filtering, VecDeque::retain is the ring-buffer equivalent, and HashMap/HashSet::retain remove per entry without compaction. Use the explicit drain/filter/collect form only when the vector is shared behind an Arc and the mutation has to produce a new allocation.
pitfalls: retain keeps where the predicate returns true, the opposite acceptance of a remove_if-style API: porting remove_if(pred) as retain(pred) inverts the result and keeps exactly the wrong elements.

The closure may borrow other state but not the vector itself: mutating v inside it does not compile, and reproducing an erase-in-loop with index juggling fights the borrow checker instead of using retain.
retain is scan-and-drop: it cannot hand the removed values back and drops them when the call ends - use extract_if when their ownership matters.
sources: doc.rust-lang.org, Vec::retain (stable since 1.0.0) - 'Retains only the elements specified by the predicate. In other words, remove all elements e for which f(&e) returns false. This method operates in place, visiting each element exactly once in the original order, and preserves the order of the retained elements'; retain_mut (1.61.0) is documented alongside it: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.retain

variants.name: Vec::extract_if (draining iterator that moves removed elements out)
variants.implementation_notes: extract_if (stable since Rust 1.87) returns a draining iterator instead of dropping: 'If the closure returns true, the element is removed from the vector and yielded', and the vector is compacted as the iterator advances, so both halves of the idiom happen while the removed values are consumed - useful for logging, recycling, or moving them into another collection (extract_if(.., pred).for_each(drop) is the range-limited retain). Only elements inside the given range are considered, but any elements after the range still have to move if anything was extracted. Choose it over retain when the removed values themselves are wanted, or when the operation must be restricted to a sub-range.
pitfalls: If the returned iterator is dropped before being exhausted (an early break, or collecting only part of it), the elements it did not yield are retained in the vector - the opposite of what 'extract' suggests, and a silent difference from retain.
The closure receives &mut T and a panic inside it leaves that element in the vector; elements outside the range are never considered even though the tail after the range still moves.
sources: doc.rust-lang.org, Vec::extract_if (stable since Rust 1.87.0) - 'Creates an iterator which uses a closure to determine if an element in the range should be removed. If the closure returns true, the element is removed from the vector and yielded'; an iterator that is not exhausted leaves the remaining elements in place: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/vec/struct.Vec.html#method.extract_if
